chunks: As for what Abu Hashim said, that it is for worldly benefits,
it is far-fetched, because it is an obligatory act of worship, and if it were for a worldly benefit, it would not be obligatory.

Besides, enforcing the penalties in his view, in the manner of requital and legal punishment, is part of Divine punishment, and some of it has been brought forward in this life for the benefit it contains. So how can he say, despite that, that it is for worldly benefits?
Therefore, what they said is invalid.
ai.seo_question: Why are Islamic penal codes considered obligatory acts of worship rather than just worldly benefits?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi refutes Abu Hashim’s reduction of hudud to mere worldly expediency by asserting that penal codes are obligatory acts of worship (ibadat), which necessitates their divine origin rather than utilitarian design. He clarifies that while some punishments are delayed or manifested in this world for specific wisdoms, their primary status as worship proves they are not solely for temporal benefit, thereby invalidating the opposing view.

en.sayyid-athar-husain-s-h-rizvi: As for Abu Hashim’s view that penal codes are for worldly benefits,
it is unacceptable; because penal codes are obligatory acts of worship, and if they were for sheer worldly benefits, they would not be obligatory.

Besides, he believes that enforcing the penalties falls in the category of requitals, and legal penalties are part of Divine punishment, some of which have been brought in this life for certain expediencies. How can he still say that they are for worldly expediencies?
